beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book treats that absence as a structural temptation for present institutions.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Building for tomorrow can be beneficial, so borrowing from the future is not inherently wrong.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The question is what inheritance accompanies the obligations and depleted options.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Reversibility matters because some experiments permit correction while others close possibilities for everyone.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The author asks for stronger restraint as irreversible exposure widens.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The chapter develops that judgment without claiming an exact date for a civilization's collapse.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book takes the promise of technological abundance seriously, including cheaper intelligence.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: It also asks whether cheaper capability can make unsatisfied appetite more effective.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Relative status and control do not disappear simply because material production improves.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Nor does greater technical ability automatically supply legitimacy for its use.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Judgment can become a tighter bottleneck as actions become easier to produce.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: This is where the discussion connects economic incentives to technological governance.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The question is what greater power requires from the institutions directing it.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: A brake preserves possibilities by refusing part of the momentum available now.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The final chapters use that image to make restraint into collective technology.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Safety margins, independent checks and credible stopping conditions all have real costs.
